summary: Defines SNMP management objects for bridges that support traffic classes, multicast filtering and virtual LANs. It was replaced by RFC 4363.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for network switches that handle traffic priorities, multicast filtering, and virtual LANs.

tldr.problem: Network switches have become more sophisticated, supporting traffic class prioritization, advanced multicast filtering, and virtual LANs. The original bridge MIB (RFC 1493) did not cover these new capabilities, making them impossible to manage via SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines two new MIB modules: an Extended Bridge MIB for IEEE 802.1D-1998 traffic class and multicast enhancements, and a Virtual Bridge MIB for IEEE 802.1Q VLAN support. Together they provide managed objects for configuring and monitoring priorities, filtering, and VLAN membership.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can now monitor and configure advanced switch features such as traffic priority queuing, multicast group registration, and VLAN assignments via standard SNMP. The RFC was replaced by RFC 4363.

today: RFC 2674 was a Proposed Standard defining SNMP management objects for advanced bridge features. It was obsoleted by RFC 4363, which updated the VLAN and bridge management specifications.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network bridges (switches) forward frames between LAN segments. The original bridge MIB (RFC 1493) covered basic bridging, but modern switches support much more. IEEE 802.1D-1998 added support for traffic classes (assigning priority to packets) and enhanced multicast filtering (controlling which multicast addresses go where). IEEE 802.1Q-1998 added Virtual LANs (VLANs), which let a single physical switch behave as multiple logical switches.

This RFC defines SNMP managed objects (a MIB) for all these new features. Network administrators can now use standard SNMP tools to read statistics, configure priorities, manage multicast group memberships, and set up and monitor VLANs. The RFC defines two MIB modules: one for traffic classes and multicast enhancements (P-BRIDGE-MIB) and one for VLAN management (Q-BRIDGE-MIB).
sections.plainLanguage: A network switch used to be simple: forward or block each message. Now switches can read the importance label and handle important messages faster, filter multicast carefully, and organize traffic into separate virtual networks. This RFC explains how to manage all of that with SNMP.

sections.title: Traffic Classes, Multicast, and VLANs
sections.content:
Traffic Classes: Switches can assign incoming frames to one of several priority queues. The RFC defines objects to configure per-port user priorities, map incoming priority values to internal traffic classes, and control outbound priority. The dot1dPriority group manages priority-based queuing mechanisms, including a User Priority Regeneration Table that remaps incoming priorities and a Traffic Class Table that maps priorities to classes.

Multicast Filtering: Switches can limit which ports multicast addresses reach using GARP (Generic Attribute Registration Protocol) and GMRP (GARP Multicast Registration Protocol). The RFC defines objects in dot1dGarp and dot1dGmrp groups to configure and report on these protocols, including timers and failed registrations.

Virtual LANs: VLANs allow a switch to partition traffic into isolated domains. The Q-BRIDGE-MIB module (Virtual Bridge MIB) defines the dot1qVlan group, which manages VLAN configuration including VLAN IDs, egress port membership, tagging rules, and static filtering entries per VLAN.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a post office where some mail gets the fast lane (traffic classes), some multicast newsletters only go to certain zip codes (multicast filtering), and some companies get their own private post office (VLANs). This RFC says how to manage all three.

sections.title: MIB Module Organization
sections.content:
The Extended Bridge MIB (P-BRIDGE-MIB) contains six main groups: dot1dExtBase (device-wide traffic class capabilities), dot1dPriority (per-port and per-priority configuration), dot1dGarp (GARP timing and status), dot1dGmrp (multicast registration protocol), dot1dTpHCPortTable (high-capacity port statistics for busy switches), and dot1dTpPortOverflowTable (overflow counters for ultra-busy ports).

The Virtual Bridge MIB (Q-BRIDGE-MIB) focuses on VLAN management: dot1qBase (VLAN version and maximum VLANs), dot1qTp (dynamic and static filtering databases per VLAN), dot1qStatic (static unicast and multicast entries), dot1qVlan (VLAN configuration and statistics), and dot1qPortVlan (per-port VLAN membership and ingress filtering).

Objects reference IEEE standard tables: Priority Regeneration, Traffic Classes, GARP registration timers, and GMRP status. The MIB scales efficiently, allowing managers to work with large numbers of ports and VLANs without overwhelming the switch.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch exposes different dials and gauges depending on what you want to manage: priority queues, multicast filters, or VLANs. Each has its own group of dials in the management interface.

sections.title: Interoperability and High-Capacity Support
sections.content:
The RFC is designed to work with existing transparent bridging standards while adding new capabilities. The dot1qPortCapabilitiesTable lets managers discover which advanced features a port supports: tagging (802.1Q VLAN support), configurable frame acceptance rules, and ingress filtering.

For high-speed and large-capacity switches, the RFC includes special groups. dot1dTpHCPortTable provides 64-bit counters for frame counts and discards, necessary when 32-bit counters would overflow within seconds on a 10+ Gbps link. dot1dTpPortOverflowTable provides overflow counter extensions so managers can sum multiple counters to recover the true count without missing updates.

The VLAN module includes per-VLAN port statistics, per-VLAN traffic counters, and learning constraint tables to prevent certain VLANs from learning media access control addresses on certain ports. Managers can enable GVRP (GARP VLAN Registration Protocol) on ports to allow switches to dynamically register VLAN memberships.
sections.plainLanguage: For very busy switches, the RFC provides larger counters that do not overflow as easily. It also lets the manager ask a port "do you support 802.1Q tagging?" before trying to use it.
